Well-designed dual-timescale temporal modeling combining rolling KV-cache (local coherence) and joint visual guidance (global coherence)
Thoughtful training strategy with patch-wise pixel supervision and cross-chunk distribution matching balancing fidelity, consistency, and memory efficiency
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (fidelity, perceptual quality, pixel-level and semantic-level consistency), extensive ablations, and 7 baseline comparisons

Strong empirical results achieving top-1 or top-2 performance across diverse datasets and metrics; linear runtime scaling and constant memory enable practical deployment

Limited generalization analysis: all experiments use ×4 upscaling only; no evaluation on other scales (2×, 8×) or different video types; no failure case analysis

Reproducibility concerns: code link unavailable at review time; method depends on non-public Wan 2.1 model; some implementation details unclear (exact DiT modifications, reference frame selection strategy)
Incomplete technical justification: why (3,3) chunk/cache size is optimal lacks theoretical explanation; reference frame selection (middle frame 'e.g.') not specified; sensitivity analysis absent

strengths: Addresses practical problem of long-form video super-resolution with clear motivation for efficiency and scalability limitations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets and metrics, including new semantic-level consistency measures from VBench
Achieves significant practical speedups (58× over MGLD-VSR) with constant memory consumption, demonstrating genuine efficiency gains
Well-designed technical approach combining rolling KV-cache and joint visual guidance with sensible motivation for the VSR setting
Introduces MovieLQ benchmark and provides thorough ablation studies (Table 4) validating design choices
Solid engineering execution with two-stage curriculum training and patch-wise supervision effectively addressing training challenges
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (KV-cache from LLMs, visual prompting, patch-wise loss, DMD, two-stage training); AR-OSD is relatively straightforward combination without substantial conceptual innovation

Insufficient validation of 'unbounded-length' claims: tested only up to 100 frames in ablations, MovieLQ uses 1000 frames; no evidence of error accumulation or how method scales to truly long sequences (e.g., 10K+ frames)
Marginal semantic consistency improvements lack statistical significance: Table 2 shows <0.1% differences in VBench metrics; unclear if improvements are meaningful vs. noise
Incomplete code availability (blank placeholder statement) and insufficient reproducibility details on T2V adaptation, training time, and implementation specifics
Unclear mechanistic justification for length generalization: why would chunk size (3,3) learned on short videos generalize to arbitrary lengths? No analysis provided

Questionable baseline comparison fairness on MovieLQ: using progressive patch aggregation for baselines may handicap methods not designed for this approach; unclear if this is optimal inference mode for each method
DMD loss introduces quality-consistency trade-off (PSNR 25.04→24.86, Table 4e) without thorough discussion of when this trade-off is appropriate

Limited analysis of failure modes and error accumulation: no ablation on performance degradation beyond 100 frames, no study of chunk boundary artifacts, single example in Figure 5 for temporal stability
Narrow experimental scope: only ×4 upscaling tested; generalization to other upscaling factors unclear; no user studies validating perceptual improvements

Design choices under-justified: why middle frame only for visual guidance? Table 4b shows marginal improvement from joint vs. separate guidance; limited sensitivity analysis for (3,3) chunk/cache size

strengths: Addresses a significant practical problem: existing VSR methods fundamentally cannot process long videos due to memory constraints and temporal decomposition artifacts. The 58× speedup over MGLD-VSR and constant memory usage are substantial practical improvements.

Technically sound architecture with well-motivated design choices: rolling KV-cache maintains local smoothness while joint visual guidance leverages LR as global prior. Patch-wise pixel supervision elegantly enables high-resolution training under memory constraints.

Comprehensive experimental validation across 5 datasets with multiple metric types (fidelity: PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, perceptual: MUSIQ/CLIP-IQA, temporal: E_warp and semantic VBench metrics). Thorough ablation studies (Table 4a-e) validate each design component.
Strong semantic consistency demonstrated through VBench metrics (BC, SC, MS), addressing a critical gap in VSR evaluation beyond pixel-level metrics. This is valuable for practical deployment.
MovieLQ benchmark fills a real evaluation gap for long-form VSR, enabling assessment on 1000-frame sequences with real-world degradation. First adoption of semantic-level consistency metrics for VSR.

Efficient and scalable design with linear runtime scaling and constant memory per chunk, enabling practical streaming inference for unbounded-length videos—a significant advantage over existing methods.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental methodological novelty: each core component (AR-diffusion, one-step distillation, KV-cache, distribution matching) is adapted from prior work. The contribution is primarily integration for VSR rather than novel algorithmic innovation.

Mixed performance on standard quality metrics: SeedVR2 outperforms on PSNR (25.38 vs 24.86) and SSIM (0.7764 vs 0.7274) on UDM10; STAR achieves lower E_warp on MVSR4x. Method excels in efficiency and semantic consistency but not uniformly on quality.

Insufficient justification for design choices: Why (3,3) for chunk/cache? Ablation Table 4c shows (5,5) yields only marginal gains. Claim that patch-wise loss is 'expectationally equivalent' to full-video loss lacks formal proof. Information loss from KV-cache truncation not quantified.

MovieLQ benchmark underspecified: total number of videos not stated, ground-truth degradation protocol not detailed, dataset availability unclear. Progressive patch aggregation applied to baselines could introduce bias favoring InfVSR's chunk-based design.

No human evaluation: Claims about 'visual quality' and 'perceptual coherence' rely entirely on automated metrics, which may not correlate with human perception. User study would strengthen quality claims.

Incomplete long-form validation: 'Unbounded-length' capability claimed but efficiency table (Table 3) only tests up to 100 frames; MovieLQ at 1000 frames is modest for validation. Behavior on 10,000+ frame videos unknown.
Two-stage training adds reproducibility burden: why is Stage I pretraining necessary? Could end-to-end training work? This complexity is practical but not well justified theoretically.

Limited generalization analysis: trained only on REDS with synthetic degradations. No cross-dataset or novel degradation type evaluation. Generalization to real-world out-of-distribution scenarios unclear.

strengths: Novel AR-OSD formulation specifically designed for streaming VSR with dual-timescale conditioning (KV-cache + joint guidance) for maintaining temporal coherence
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets with strong results: state-of-the-art quality on UDM10/MovieLQ, 58× speedup over MGLD-VSR, effective temporal consistency preservation
Valuable MovieLQ benchmark contribution addressing gap for evaluating true long-form VSR (1000-frame sequences with real-world degradations)
Technically sound methodology with detailed mathematical formulation, clear architecture design, comprehensive ablation studies, and reproducibility through promised code release
Honest treatment of limitations including computational constraints, training scale restrictions, and dependence on pretrained priors; transparent discussion of future improvements
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why AR-OSD specifically optimizes temporal consistency; connection between autoregressive formulation and coherence is empirically validated but lacks principled explanation
Critical dependence on pretrained T2V diffusion priors; improvements may partially reflect prior quality rather than proposed methodology; limited ablation on sensitivity to prior strength

Temporal consistency improvements often modest in magnitude (e.g., VBench SC 0.9578 vs 0.9456); error accumulation over very long sequences (>1000 frames) not thoroughly analyzed despite claims about avoiding degradation
Limited algorithmic novelty—individual components (DIT, VAE, distribution matching) from existing work; contribution primarily in system design/engineering rather than new techniques

MovieLQ benchmark limited to ~10 single-shot 1000-frame videos; small validation set for drawing strong generalization conclusions; streaming capability evaluated mainly on fixed sequences rather than true streaming scenarios

Design choices lack clear justification: optimal KV-cache length M=3 shown in ablation (Table 7) but not explained in main text; cross-chunk distribution matching loss motivation unclear; loss weight ratios unexplained
Concurrent streaming methods (FlashVSR, Stream-DiffVSR) relegated to appendix; main comparisons against mostly non-streaming baselines, reducing evaluation comprehensiveness

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem (long-sequence video super-resolution with temporal consistency constraints)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (UDM10, MVSR4K, MovieLQ, SPMCS) with consistent improvements in PSNR and perceptual metrics
Introduces MovieLQ, a new benchmark dataset for long-form VSR evaluation with semantic-level consistency metrics
Thorough ablation studies examining key components (intra-chunk diffusion, inter-chunk autoregression, KV-cache, DMD loss)
Demonstrates practical efficiency gains with significantly reduced inference time compared to multi-step baselines
Well-organized presentation with extensive supplementary materials including implementation details and additional analysis
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (autoregressive diffusion, KV-cache from LLMs, standard KL divergence regularization) without fundamental innovation; the AR-OSD approach is an incremental application rather than a new conceptual contribution

Insufficient justification for core design choices: the paper does not rigorously explain why autoregressive inference avoids consistency degradation in long sequences (brief appendix mention is inadequate), nor does it justify why cross-chunk KL distribution matching is optimal

Presentation clarity issues: dense methodology with key details (streaming pipeline, algorithm) relegated to appendix; unclear relationship between intra-chunk and inter-chunk mechanisms; notation inconsistencies (P_k derivation vague)

Overclaimed results: '58× speedup' compares single-step vs. multi-step methods (expected), and 'SOTA' claims lack careful substantiation; comparison with concurrent streaming methods (FlashVSR, Stream-DiffVSR) shows mixed results and is confined to appendix

Experimental concerns: modest and inconsistent gains (often 0.3-0.5 dB PSNR); no statistical significance testing; MovieLQ benchmark is small (1000 clips) with unclear relevance to real VSR challenges; semantic metrics borrowed from VBench may not capture VSR-specific consistency issues

Incomplete analysis of failure modes: paper presents primarily successful examples; does not adequately examine when/where the method fails or demonstrate perceptual consistency improvements translate to semantic consistency

Reproducibility gaps: complex multi-loss training with multiple hyperparameters (λ_mse, λ_dis, λ_dmd) and two-stage curriculum hard to reproduce; missing details on pretrained T2V initialization; Table 4b suggests Stage-1 only provides marginal gains despite added complexity

Limited technical depth: temporal consistency loss (Eq. 5) equates smoothness with consistency (problematic assumption); patch supervision window size (8×) unjustified; no theoretical analysis of error accumulation or consistency guarantees

Narrow baseline selection: comparisons focus on MGLD-VSR, STAR, SeedVR; missing comparisons with compression-based and other efficient long-video methods; potential fairness issues in training data/inference setup

strengths: Novel AR-OSD formulation for streaming generative video super-resolution with well-motivated consistency constraints via dual-timescale curriculum training
Significant practical contribution: achieves 58× speedup over existing methods (MGLD-VSR) while maintaining or improving visual quality across multiple metrics
Comprehensive evaluation with new MovieLQ benchmark (1000 1K-frame videos) and semantic-level consistency metrics (SC, BC, MS) that address an important gap in long-form VSR evaluation
Strong empirical results: consistently ranks top-1 or top-2 on RealBasicVSR, ECCY, CYPR, ICCV, SPMCS datasets across diverse metrics (PSNR, LPIPS, DISTS, MUSIQ, CLIP-IQA)
Clever technical innovations: rolling KV-cache mechanism for local smoothness while preserving global coherence, effective joint visual guidance strategy using LR frames as semantic anchors
Extensive ablation studies (Table 4) convincingly validate each component, demonstrating the contribution of AR chunking, guidance strategy, stage-1 pretraining, DMD loss, and KV-cache design
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation details, clear algorithm pseudocode, training hyperparameters, and explicit mention of code/model availability
Honest treatment of limitations acknowledging training scale constraints, reliance on pretrained priors, and architectural redundancy with forward-looking discussion of improvements
weaknesses: Incremental contribution that effectively combines existing techniques (autoregressive generation, diffusion-based VSR, transformer KV-caching) rather than introducing fundamentally novel concepts
Heavy reliance on pretrained T2V diffusion models and VAE components limits the degree of innovation and may obscure the contribution of the proposed methods
Limited scope: all primary experiments restricted to 4× upscaling; generalization to other upscaling factors (2×, 8×) is not demonstrated
Incomplete comparison with concurrent streaming VSR methods: Stream-DiffVSR and FlashVSR comparison is relegated to appendix (Table 10) with limited analysis despite their relevance
Temporal smoothness loss (Eq. 5) based on simple pixel-level frame differences may miss higher-order temporal structure; limited exploration of alternative temporal regularization approaches
KV-cache hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: while Table 7 provides ablation for cache length M, the selection of M=3 as default is not clearly motivated
Evaluation on MovieLQ uses 1000-frame videos; claims about 'unbounded-length sequences' may be overstated—true unbounded evaluation would strengthen the contribution
Limited discussion of failure modes and scenarios where the method underperforms; no analysis of sensitivity to different video content types or degradation patterns
